neighbours.label: pairing in twos, especially electrons pairing in an orbital (each orbital holds two electrons with opposite spins)
fire: In a covalent bond, the two atoms share a pair of electrons.
Every orbital can be occupied by at most two electrons of opposite spin.
The lone pair on the nitrogen atom makes ammonia a weak base.
Electrons fill each orbital singly before they begin to pair up.
A helium atom has its two electrons paired in the 1s orbital.
Paired electrons cancel each other's magnetic moments out.
Oxygen has two unpaired electrons, which makes it paramagnetic.
Shoes, gloves and earrings are usually sold in pairs at the market.
quiet: In a covalent bond, the atoms are held together by attraction.
Every orbital has a characteristic shape and a fixed energy.
The nitrogen atom makes ammonia a weak base in water.
Electrons fill each shell in order of increasing energy.
A helium atom is very stable and rarely reacts.
Charged particles move faster in a strong magnetic field.
Oxygen has a high electronegativity, which makes it reactive.
Shoes, hats and scarves are usually sold by size at the market.
